newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Vranitzky in dock after far right soars in poll.
newsitem.headline: Vranitzky in dock after far right soars in poll.

text.p: Austria's first European parliamentary poll brought a clear vote of no-confidence in Chancellor Franz Vranitzky while huge far right gains showed a people longing for change, newspapers said on Monday.
Many domestic newspapers said Vranitzky's 10-year grip on the reins of government had loosened after his Social Democratic Party suffered its worst result in Austria's democratic history on Sunday.
"A slap in the face for the Social Democrats: When will Vranitzky step down?" asked the headline in the right-leaning Kleine Zeitung.

"This vote was not just a protest vote. It was a farewell to Franz Vranitzky from the voters...A change in the Social Democratic leadership and at the chancellery looks unavoidable," wrote the normally sober Kurier in a commentary.

While the Social Democrats suffered the humiliation of finishing second to junior coalition partner the conservative People's Party, Joerg Haider's nationalist Freedom Party scored its biggest triumph to date.
"There has been a significant change in Austria's psychological and political landscape. This result shows voters are increasingly willing to put Joerg Haider in government," wrote Der Standard.
The People's Party won 29.6 percent of the vote, followed by the Social Democrats on 29.1 percent.
The far-right notched up 27.6 percent, its best result in a nationwide election and a huge jump from the five percent it commanded when Haider took over the party 10 years ago.

The result gives the People's Party seven of Austria's 21 seats in the European Parliament. The Social Democrats and Freedom Party will occupy six seats each, while the leftist Greens and Liberals take one apiece.

Newspapers on Monday were unanimous that voters had expressed their frustration at domestic economic policies and a tough austerity budget more than a disgruntlement over European integration and a single currency.
"Sunday's vote was not a vote for the Austrian parliament. Nevertheless, government policy was in the dock," Der Standard said.
Vranitzky was taking the blame for all the Alpine republic's economic ills, newspapers decided.

He drew the ire of pensioners by reneging on a promise that their income would be safe from government austerity measures. Austrian workers felt betrayed by an influx of foreigners and a wave of job losses, newspapers said.
"It has been the fatal tactic of our government to export jobs abroad while importing foreigners who live on welfare," wrote the rightist Neue Kronen Zeitung, Austria's biggest circulation daily.
Haider had succeeded in reaching the hearts and minds of ordinary Austrians, stealing the Social Democrats' traditional role as a party of the workers.
"For a proud movement that is a tragedy," concluded Der Standard.
